editorial_proposal.description_short: SSA said it had not permanently closed or announced closing any local field office since Jan. 1, 2025, while noting one announced hearing-office closure in White Plains.
editorial_proposal.description_medium: On March 27, 2025, the Social Security Administration said it had not permanently closed or announced closing any local field office since Jan. 1. The agency said it had announced one hearing-office closure in White Plains, New York. It also said many spaces submitted to GSA for possible lease termination were small hearing rooms without assigned employees.
editorial_proposal.description_long: On March 27, 2025, the Social Security Administration said it had not permanently closed or announced the permanent closure of any local field office since Jan. 1 of that year. The agency separately said it had announced one hearing-office closure in White Plains, New York. SSA said it works with congressional delegations before permanent closures and reassigns employees from affected offices to other locations. It also said many spaces submitted to the General Services Administration for possible lease termination were small hearing rooms without assigned employees, as most hearings were held virtually. The agency said temporary local-office closures can occur because of weather, damage or facilities problems, followed by reopening. The statement distinguishes local field offices from a hearing office and small hearing rooms. It does not establish that DOGE closed ten local offices or that the White Plains decision resulted from DOGE.

children_proposals.title: Rescissions Act cancels future Corporation for Public Broadcasting appropriations
children_proposals.description_short: The Rescissions Act of 2025 rescinded Corporation for Public Broadcasting appropriations for fiscal years 2026 and 2027, effective upon enactment on July 24, 2025.
children_proposals.description_medium: President Donald Trump signed the Rescissions Act of 2025 on July 24, 2025. Section 2 made the act’s rescissions effective upon enactment and rescinded Corporation for Public Broadcasting amounts made available for fiscal years 2026 and 2027. The statute establishes those appropriations rescissions; it does not state a $1.1 billion total or quantify station-level losses.
children_proposals.description_long: President Donald Trump signed the Rescissions Act of 2025 on July 24, 2025, following a June 3 presidential rescission request. The enacted statute says the rescissions took effect upon enactment. Section 2(b)(20) identifies and rescinds amounts made available to the Corporation for Public Broadcasting for fiscal years 2026 and 2027, including amounts provided through the Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2024, and the Full-Year Continuing Appropriations and Extensions Act, 2025. This was a statutory cancellation of specified future CPB appropriations. The law does not state that $1.1 billion was cut and does not quantify effects on individual public television or radio stations. Those amounts and downstream effects require separate appropriations records or station-level evidence. The text identifies the fiscal-year appropriations it rescinded and makes that rescission effective upon enactment; it does not itself report station receipts, local programming changes or individual broadcaster losses.

facts: The act took effect on enactment, July 24, 2025.

editorial_proposal.description_long: An Associated Press report published April 18, 2017, said Ivanka Trump’s company received provisional approval from China on April 6 for three trademarks covering jewelry, bags and spa services. The report distinguished the three approvals announced for that date from the wider trademark portfolio: it said the company then had 16 registered trademarks in China and 32 pending applications, and that four marks had received preliminary approval since the inauguration. The report also discussed the family’s stated ethics safeguards and concerns raised by former government ethics officials about business and policy overlap. This proposal records the specifically reported approval and dinner chronology. The timing alone does not establish that the dinner influenced the trademark decisions, and the 16 registered marks should not be presented as 16 approvals issued on April 6.

editorial_proposal.title: White House officials used Signal to discuss Yemen operations
editorial_proposal.description_short: In March 2025, senior Trump administration officials used Signal to discuss military operations in Yemen in a group chat that included a journalist.
editorial_proposal.description_medium: In March 2025, senior Trump administration officials used Signal in a group chat to discuss planned military operations in Yemen. The chat accidentally included journalist Jeffrey Goldberg, who later reported on the messages. Reuters reported that officials said steps had been taken to prevent a recurrence. The reporting documents a specific Signal-use incident, not a government-wide ban on encrypted messaging.
editorial_proposal.description_long: In March 2025, senior Trump administration officials used Signal to discuss planned U.S. military operations in Yemen in a group chat that accidentally included a journalist. Reuters reported that the thread described an imminent bombing campaign against Houthi militants in Yemen. Jeffrey Goldberg of The Atlantic was added to the private chat alongside Vice President JD Vance, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth and CIA Director John Ratcliffe. Goldberg disclosed the messages publicly on March 24. On March 31, White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt said the White House considered the case closed and that steps had been taken to prevent recurrence. Reuters also reported that House Intelligence Committee Democrats requested an independent inquiry and leaders of the Senate Armed Services Committee asked the Pentagon to investigate the leak. The reporting concerns this specific Signal thread; it does not establish a government-wide ban on Signal, WhatsApp or other encrypted messaging apps.

The coverage reported that the Trump family has a financial interest in World Liberty Financial and described concerns about Trump-appointed banking regulators overseeing a family-linked company. Those are conflict concerns raised by critics, not a finding that officials acted improperly. The event is a conditional regulatory step; the company’s final charter and actual operations were unresolved in the reports.

editorial_proposal.description_long: On August 18, 2026, The New Republic reported that the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency had granted preliminary conditional approval to World Liberty Financial’s application for a national trust bank called World Liberty Trust Company. The article stated that the Trump family owned 38 percent of World Liberty Financial and received 75 percent of the company’s cryptocurrency revenue. The OCC approval was not permission to open: the applicant still had to raise capital, satisfy other conditions and complete pre-opening review. The New Republic says the Trump family holds a substantial ownership stake in World Liberty Financial and receives revenue from its cryptocurrency business. It argues that the approval raises a conflict because the family could benefit from a company receiving federal banking approval under an administration led by Trump. Those ownership details and the conflict argument are claims reported in the article, not a finding of misconduct. The event is the regulator’s preliminary approval; the article’s corruption characterization is opinion. The charter process remained incomplete in the report.

The company still had to satisfy capital, governance and pre-opening requirements before it could conduct business; the letter did not authorize it to operate as a bank. Reporting raised conflict concerns but identified no finding of misconduct.
editorial_proposal.description_long: The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency issued preliminary conditional approval for World Liberty Trust Company to pursue a national trust bank charter in August 2026. The OCC letter states that this step is not final approval and that the company may not begin banking business until it meets specified conditions and receives the agency’s final approval. Requirements include raising capital, establishing compliance and information-security policies, obtaining other regulatory approvals and requesting a pre-opening examination. If capital is not raised within 12 months or the bank does not open within 18 months, the preliminary approval expires. HuffPost reported the approval as a development involving World Liberty Financial, the cryptocurrency company associated with the Trump family. The reports raised conflict-of-interest concerns because of that family connection, but the OCC letter does not find misconduct or say the company was already operating. The event is a conditional licensing step; whether the applicant will satisfy the requirements and receive a final charter remained unresolved.
